## Overview

Ecological Bayesian networks are often built first as descriptions of a system, and a
management decision is added later [@Marcot2006; @Runge2011]. The usual way to add it is
to edit the network into one larger influence diagram. With open influence diagrams the
network can stay as it was published: it is opened at a boundary, a separate component
holds the decision, its cost and how it acts on the system, and the pieces are composed.
The decision then sees exactly what the boundary declares observed, and nothing else.

This vignette does that with the reference habitat network of the model zoo of
`EcologicalBayesianNetworks.jl`. The network models soil moisture from climate and
irrigation, and the vegetation, habitat quality and occupancy of a species from soil
moisture and grazing pressure. In the zoo the grazing pressure is a root with a fixed
prior. Here a manager sets it instead, through a grazing decision made on the observed
soil moisture. The vignette opens the network at the boundary, attaches the decision
component, composes, optimises the closed composite, and then optimises the decision
component on its own against the context the network induces on its boundary.

## Setup

`load_model` builds a model of the zoo. The reference habitat network is built into the
zoo under the MIT licence, so it needs no download, and so is the SPEC section 46 grazing
diagram, from which the decision component borrows its numbers.

```{julia}
using CategoricalInfluenceDiagrams
using EcologicalBayesianNetworks

zoo = ["reference_habitat_bn", "reference_grazing_id"]
[(name, model_info(name).licence, model_info(name).redistribution) for name in zoo]
```

```{julia}
habitat = load_model("reference_habitat_bn")
grazing = load_model("reference_grazing_id")
[x => states(syntax(habitat), x) for x in variable_names(syntax(habitat))]
```

```{julia}
to_graphviz(syntax(habitat))
```

The kernels of the zoo network, keyed by variable name, are the tables every component
below reads:

```{julia}
zoo_kernels = Dict{Symbol,FiniteKernel}(x => kernel(habitat, x)
                                        for x in variable_names(syntax(habitat)))
zoo_kernels[:GrazingPressure]
```

## Opening the zoo network at a boundary

Cut the network at soil moisture and grazing pressure, the two parents of vegetation.
Upstream of the cut is the abiotic part, which generates soil moisture; downstream is the
biotic part, which reads soil moisture and grazing pressure and generates vegetation,
habitat quality and occupancy. Grazing pressure is generated by its own prior, a third
piece. In the biotic part both cut variables are exogenous (`closed = false`), so they
can be inputs.

```{julia}
abiotic = bayesnet(:Climate => [:dry, :normal, :wet], :Irrigation => [:low, :high],
                   :SoilMoisture => [:low, :medium, :high];
                   mechanisms = [:SoilMoisture => (:Climate, :Irrigation)])
pressure_prior = bayesnet(:GrazingPressure => [:low, :high])
biotic = bayesnet(:SoilMoisture => [:low, :medium, :high], :GrazingPressure => [:low, :high],
                  :Vegetation => [:sparse, :moderate, :dense],
                  :HabitatQuality => [:poor, :good], :Occupancy => [:absent, :present];
                  mechanisms = [:Vegetation => (:SoilMoisture, :GrazingPressure),
                                :HabitatQuality => :Vegetation,
                                :Occupancy => :HabitatQuality],
                  closed = false)
nothing # hide
```

As open influence diagrams the three pieces have no decisions and no utilities. Placing
the abiotic part beside the prior (`⊗`) and composing with the biotic part (`⋅`) glues
the network back together, and the result is the zoo network again:

```{julia}
E0 = Open(InfluenceDiagram(abiotic); outputs = [:SoilMoisture])
P0 = Open(InfluenceDiagram(pressure_prior); outputs = [:GrazingPressure])
H0 = Open(InfluenceDiagram(biotic); inputs = [:SoilMoisture, :GrazingPressure],
          outputs = [:Occupancy])
N = (E0 ⊗ P0) ⋅ H0
println(N)
canonicalize(apex(OpenBayesNet(N))) == canonicalize(reference_habitat_bn())
```

The semantics agrees too. Under the empty strategy the reward kernel of `N` has zero
reward, and its probability part is the zoo model's marginal of occupancy:

```{julia}
rN = interpret(N, zoo_kernels, Dict{Symbol,AbstractUtility}(), Strategy())
kernel(rN) ≈ marginal(habitat, :Occupancy), all(iszero, reward(rN))
```

## A management component and a valuation component

The manager replaces the prior on grazing pressure. The management component holds a
decision, `GrazingManagement` (exclude, reduce or maintain grazing), made on the soil
moisture; a mechanism for the grazing pressure that the decision achieves; and the cost
of the decision. It takes the soil moisture as an observed input and passes it on, with
the grazing pressure, to the biotic part. What the manager observed is information for the
decision, and the biotic part has no decision to inform, so the soil moisture leaves the
component hidden: `observed` takes a named tuple that flags each foot separately, and here
names the soil moisture on the input foot only. The kernel of the grazing pressure and the cost are those of the
zoo's SPEC section 46 grazing diagram: excluding grazing makes low pressure likely but
not certain, and costs 40, reducing it costs 15, maintaining it nothing.

```{julia}
management = influence_diagram(:SoilMoisture => [:low, :medium, :high],
                               :GrazingManagement => [:exclude, :reduce, :maintain],
                               :GrazingPressure => [:low, :high];
                               mechanisms = [:GrazingPressure => :GrazingManagement],
                               decisions = [:GrazingManagement => :SoilMoisture],
                               utilities = [:ManagementCost => :GrazingManagement],
                               closed = false)
M = Open(management; inputs = [:SoilMoisture],
         outputs = [:SoilMoisture, :GrazingPressure],
         observed = (inputs = [:SoilMoisture],))
println(M)
utility_table(bound_utilities(grazing)[:ManagementCost])
```

A valuation component scores the outcome. The zoo network has no utility, so the value
of the species' presence is a choice made here: 1000 against a management cost of at most
40, a reserve that values the species highly.

```{julia}
V = Open(influence_diagram(:Occupancy => [:absent, :present];
                           utilities = [:ConservationBenefit => :Occupancy],
                           closed = false);
         inputs = [:Occupancy])
benefit(value) = TabularUtility([FiniteAxis(:Occupancy, [:absent, :present])],
                                [0.0, value])
utilities = Dict{Symbol,AbstractUtility}(:ManagementCost => bound_utilities(grazing)[:ManagementCost],
                                         :ConservationBenefit => benefit(1000.0))
println(V)
```

The kernels of the composite are those of the zoo network, except that grazing pressure
is now generated by the management decision:

```{julia}
kernels = merge(zoo_kernels, Dict(:GrazingPressure => kernel(grazing, :GrazingPressure)))
kernels[:GrazingPressure]
```

## Observability at the boundary

The decision reads the soil moisture across the boundary, so the boundary must declare it
observed. The abiotic part as opened above declares nothing observed, as `Open` does by
default, and so it does not match the management component:

```{julia}
try
    compose(E0, M)
catch e
    sprint(showerror, e)
end
```

Nor may the management component hide the soil moisture from its own decision (rule 3 of
the typed-interface rule):

```{julia}
try
    Open(management; inputs = [:SoilMoisture], outputs = [:SoilMoisture, :GrazingPressure])
catch e
    sprint(showerror, e)
end
```

So the abiotic part is opened with soil moisture observed. The management component
passes the soil moisture on hidden, so the biotic part is used exactly as it was opened
above, with everything hidden: it has no decision, and nothing downstream reads the soil
moisture as information. Grazing pressure stays hidden too: the manager chooses the
management, not the pressure it achieves. Both boundaries now match:

```{julia}
E = Open(InfluenceDiagram(abiotic); outputs = [:SoilMoisture], observed = [:SoilMoisture])
H = H0
println(E)
interface_matches(codom(E), dom(M)), interface_matches(codom(M), dom(H))
```

## Composing and optimising the closed composite

The four components compose in sequence into a closed influence diagram:

```{julia}
whole = E ⋅ M ⋅ H ⋅ V
println(whole)
```

```{julia}
to_graphviz(apex(whole); states = false)
```

Its apex is an ordinary influence diagram, so `optimize` solves it with the solvers of
`InfluenceDiagrams.jl` (decision variable elimination by default). The policy table is
indexed by the soil moisture (low, medium, high):

```{julia}
best = optimize(whole, kernels, utilities)
round(best.expected_utility; digits = 2), policy_table(best.strategy[:GrazingManagement])
```

The optimal policy reacts to the soil moisture, and it is worth more than any fixed
action:

```{julia}
fixed = [a => round(contextual_value(whole, kernels, utilities,
                                     Strategy(:GrazingManagement => ConstantPolicy(a)));
                    digits = 2)
         for a in (:exclude, :reduce, :maintain)]
```

With a lower value on the species' presence the decision is not worth taking. Valued at
100, the cost of management is never repaid and the optimal policy maintains grazing
whatever the soil moisture:

```{julia}
low_value = merge(utilities, Dict(:ConservationBenefit => benefit(100.0)))
policy_table(optimize(whole, kernels, low_value).strategy[:GrazingManagement])
```

## Optimising the decision component in context

The management component is open: it has inputs and outputs, so it has no expected
utility of its own. It has one in a context: a law `μ` on its input and a value `c` for
each of its output states. The rest of the composite supplies both.

- `boundary_law` of `E` is the law the abiotic part induces on the soil moisture.
- `continuation_value` of `H ⋅ V` is the expected conservation benefit that the biotic
  part and the valuation earn from each joint state of soil moisture and grazing
  pressure.

```{julia}
ν = boundary_law(E, kernels, utilities, Strategy())
rHV = interpret(H ⋅ V, kernels, utilities, Strategy())
c = continuation_value(rHV)
(soil_moisture = round.(ν; digits = 3),
 continuation = [y => round(v; digits = 1)
                 for (y, v) in zip(joint_states(dom(rHV)), c)])
```

`contextual_optimize` maximises the component's value in that context over its legal
strategies, the policies that read the soil moisture. It finds the optimum of the closed
composite and the same policy:

```{julia}
local_best = contextual_optimize(M, kernels, utilities; prior = ν, continuation = c)
(local_best.expected_utility ≈ best.expected_utility,
 local_best.strategy == best.strategy, local_best.diagnostics)
```

This is the contextual identity: for every strategy `σ` of the management component, its
value in the context `(ν, c)` is the expected utility of the whole composite. The abiotic
part earns no reward of its own, so nothing is added for it.

```{julia}
all(contextual_value(M, kernels, utilities, σ; prior = ν, continuation = c) ≈
    contextual_value(whole, kernels, utilities, σ)
    for σ in (best.strategy,
              (Strategy(:GrazingManagement => ConstantPolicy(a))
               for a in (:exclude, :reduce, :maintain))...))
```

The context matters. Optimised against a zero continuation, as if nothing downstream
depended on the grazing, the component sees only the cost of management and maintains
grazing everywhere. Composed with the network, that choice is worth less than the
optimum:

```{julia}
isolated = contextual_optimize(M, kernels, utilities; prior = ν, continuation = zeros(6))
(policy = policy_table(isolated.strategy[:GrazingManagement]),
 composed_value = round(contextual_value(whole, kernels, utilities, isolated.strategy);
                        digits = 2),
 optimum = round(best.expected_utility; digits = 2))
```

Here the failure is easy to see, because the context that was left out is the whole
benefit. The third vignette,
[Why optimisation does not compose](../03_why_optimisation_does_not_compose/03_why_optimisation_does_not_compose.md),
shows that it goes wrong even when each component is optimised against the context its
neighbours actually induce, one component at a time.

## Summary

The reference habitat network of the model zoo was opened at the boundary between soil
moisture and grazing pressure and the rest of the network, and composed back to itself
with the same kernel of occupancy. Replacing the prior on grazing pressure by a management
component, with a decision on the observed soil moisture, the SPEC section 46 kernel of
achieved grazing pressure and its cost, and adding a valuation of occupancy, gave a closed
influence diagram that `optimize` solves. The boundary had to declare the soil moisture
observed where the decision reads it, on the input foot of the management component: an
embedded network hides everything, and a decision that reads a hidden input is refused.
Nothing downstream needed it, so it left the component hidden, and the biotic part of the
network was composed as it was opened. Optimised on its own against the law the network induces on its input and the
value the network earns from its outputs, the decision component attains the optimum of
the whole; optimised against a context that leaves the network out, it does not.
